The river town woke before the sun cleared the eastern ridge. Fishermen
checked their nets along the stone quay, bakers opened the shutters of shops
that had stood for four generations, and the first ferry pushed away from the
bank with a low, steady hum. By mid-morning the market square was full: farmers
selling apples and hard cheese, a clockmaker explaining a repaired movement to
a patient customer, children chasing a dog between the stalls. The town had
changed slowly, the way old buildings do, one repaired roof and one new window
at a time.

In the afternoons the wind came down the valley and carried the smell of pine
and wet stone through the streets. The mill by the weir still ground grain for
the surrounding farms, though the wheel had been rebuilt twice and the wooden
shaft replaced with steel. The miller kept a ledger of every delivery, written
in a careful hand, and on quiet days he read old entries aloud to anyone who
stopped to listen: harvests, floods, the winter the river froze, the summer the
bridge was widened.

Young people left for the city and some of them returned years later, surprised
by how little had changed and how much they had forgotten. They noticed the
cracked step outside the library, the same three bells in the tower, the same
bench where their grandparents had sat. The town did not promise them anything.
It simply waited, repaired what could be repaired, and kept its records.

On the last evening of the season, the town held its annual fair. Lanterns were
strung across the square, a small orchestra played on the steps of the hall, and
the oldest residents were given the first slices of a very large cake. Nobody
made a speech. The music continued until the lanterns burned low, and then
people walked home along the river, talking quietly, while the water carried the
reflections of the lights downstream and out of sight.
